boundary_note: Bounded first pass for the frozen Tupelo (Harrisburg) record (July 14-15, 1864) in Forrest's Defense of Mississippi [June-August 1864]: the engagement at Harrisburg near Tupelo on the 14th and the night attack, and the withdrawal and action at Old Town Creek on the 15th. The skirmishes at Pontotoc (11th-12th) and the attacks on the column on the 13th are context. Expedition-wide marches, captures, destruction and loss totals are context; they are not assigned to one record or added across records. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.rationale: No inspected return establishes matched personnel at a common opening boundary. Imported numerical estimates remain unchanged; this pass does not validate them as simultaneous opening forces.

claims.value: The frozen force field gives Smith's force as 14,000 (side bound 14,000); NPS gives Smith more than 14,000, Forrest about 6,000 at Okolona and Lee 2,000 more, and the live field reads 22000 (US 14000; CS 8000). A. J. Smith gives his aggregate on leaving La Grange as about 14,000. Forrest says his forces did not exceed 5,000 against 18,000 or 20,000; he says about 700 infantry were placed under Lyon in the reserve. Lee's dispatch gives no figures.
claims.rationale: An expedition aggregate at the start, a subordinate commander's figure for his own forces, and estimates; no matched return. None is adopted as a matched opening strength.

claims.value: Forrest says the enemy held a strong position on a ridge fronting an open field that sloped gradually toward the attackers, and had built fortifications during the night, making it almost impregnable. Smith says the enemy came on in three lines from the edge of the timber and that their dead were found within thirty yards of his batteries. Lee reported that he could not force the position.
claims.rationale: Ground and works described by the two sides' commanders; no map verification. The works were built the night before the attack, so the phase is left unresolved.

claims.value: Forrest says his scouts kept him constantly advised of the enemy's movements from La Grange, and that Smith's delay at Pontotoc gave the impression he meant to fall back toward Memphis, after which it was decided to accept battle wherever offered. Smith says he found the enemy strongly posted south of Pontotoc and chose to flank the position rather than attack it; NPS says he moved on Tupelo fearing an ambush.
claims.rationale: Knowledge and reasons stated by the commanders and a summary; no message log inspected.

claims.value: The frozen commanders are Lieutenant General Stephen D. Lee, Major General Nathan Bedford Forrest and Major General A. J. Smith. Forrest says Lee ordered the attack and the advance and directed him to swing the right against the enemy's left; that on reaching the front he found the Kentucky brigade had been rashly precipitated forward and repulsed, and did not push Roddey's command forward; that Lee later ordered him to fall back, and after his wound at Old Town Creek he ordered Chalmers to take command. Lee reported that he attacked Smith in position at Tupelo that morning. Smith says Mower advanced his lines after two hours and credits Mower's division with the hardest fighting. NPS calls the attacks a number of uncoordinated assaults ordered by Lee.
claims.rationale: Command roles from the commanders and a summary; the NPS characterization is recorded as NPS's statement. The listed commanders do not receive automatic sole credit.

claims.value: The frozen and live results read Union victory. Lee's July 14 dispatch calls the battle 'a drawn one' of three hours and says his army held a strong position. Smith says his troops drove the attackers from the field with heavy loss and returned for lack of rations and ammunition. Forrest says his troops could not carry the works and that the enemy, retreating, was driven back to his starting point.
claims.rationale: Retain the original result and engagement interval; later movements and campaign contribution are different measures. No new probabilities or individual causal credit. Lee's same-day judgment differs from the recorded result and is not adopted.

claims.value: The frozen casualty field reads 1,948 (US 648; CS 1,300); the live field reads 1973 (US 647; CS 1326). Forrest gives his loss as 210 killed and 1,116 wounded (read '1,11G' in OCR) and the enemy's as equal to his own. Smith says 270 enemy dead were counted in Mower's front, that the enemy's loss on the 14th could not fall short of 1,800, and that it would reach 3,000 killed, wounded and prisoners over the expedition; the Union casualty return (No. 3) is garbled in OCR and was not selected.
claims.rationale: Original casualty returns were not inspected; preserve totals, categories, cutoffs and differences. No canonical reconciliation or casualty-based opening count; related actions must not be added without resolving population overlap. Forrest's 210 and 1,116 sum to the live Confederate 1,326; the frozen figures have no inspected basis. Smith's 3,000 covers the whole expedition.

open_questions: Washburn's transmittal (read, not selected), the No. 3 Union casualty return (garbled), Mower's, Moore's, Grierson's and the other Union reports (Nos. 4-43), Chalmers's, Buford's and the other Confederate reports (Nos. 46-60), Jordan and Pryor's Chapter XIX and maps remain deferred.

NPS/CWSAC is one family (the NPS battle page plus the frozen Arnold rows). Nathan B. Forrest's reports of July 1 and August 4, 1864, the provost-marshal's report forwarded with the first, his June 1864 address and his August 21 Memphis dispatch as relayed by Maury (Official Records Series I, Volume XXXIX, Part 1, Nos. 22, 45 and 15) are one family of interested Confederate accounts. The Official Records volume is a shared container, not an additional witness; report dates are not event times or proof of contemporary knowledge. Here the second family is A. J. Smith's August 5, 1864 report (No. 2). As the one targeted follow-up, Stephen D. Lee's July 14 dispatch to Bragg (No. 44), the only Lee document in this expedition's report list, is a separate family for the senior Confederate commander.
No automatic commander attribution, causal campaign score, morale/readiness number or battle/campaign double counting.
